Borrowed from Russian царь (carʹ), from Old East Slavic цьсарь (cĭsarĭ), from Proto-Slavic *cěsařь, from a Germanic language, from Proto-Germanic *kaisaraz, from Latin Caesar. Doublet of Caesar and Kaiser. The spelling tsar began to replace the older czar in the nineteenth century. Compare Medieval Greek Τζαῖσαρ (Tz

s.d: a male monarch or emperor (especially of Russia prior to 1917)
(historical) An emperor of Russia (1547 to 1917) and of some South Slavic states.
x: [W]hy, in the name of common sense, should the English call the Czar (tsar) of Russia razc?
I vuz never beink too krazy about any of dose tsari.

s.d: (figuratively) A person with great power; an autocrat.

tsarina.e: Via Italian czarina or Spanish czarina, from German Czarin, Zarin, feminine form of Czar, Zar. By surface analysis, tsar + -ina.

s.d: the wife or widow of a czar
(historical) An empress of several Eastern European countries, especially Russia, or the wife of a tsar.
x: The biggest Russian czarina was Catherine the Great, a German, who incidentally made Crimea part of Russia.

tsarist.e: From tsar + -ist. Piecewise doublet of Caesarist.

tsunami.e: Borrowed from Japanese 津波 (tsunami), from 津 (tsu, “harbour”) + 波 (nami, “wave”).

s.d: a cataclysm resulting from a destructive sea wave caused by an earthquake or volcanic eruption
x: a colossal tsunami destroyed the Minoan civilization in minutes

s.d: A very large and destructive wave, generally caused by a tremendous disturbance in the ocean, such as an undersea earthquake or volcanic eruption; often a series of waves (a wave train).
x: A wave simulator in the tank can re-enact tsunamis and northeasters, and imitate wave conditions from midocean.

s.d: (figuratively) A large and generally unstoppable surge.
x: It seemed that what started out as a handful of isolated cases gradually turned into a tsunami of complaints.
It set off a tsunami of debate among the more esoteric critics, who either loved it or hated it but could not ignore it.

tsundere.e: Borrowed from Japanese ツンデレ (tsundere), from つんつん (tsun-tsun, “in a cross, aloof, or standoffish manner”, adverb) + でれでれ (dere-dere, “in a lovey-dovey, infatuated, or lovestruck manner”, adverb).

s.d: a person who is initially cold and even hostile towards another person before gradually showing a warmer side over time.
a character development process that describes a person who is initially cold and even hostile towards another person before gradually showing a warmer side over time.
A fictional character who fits the archetype of being cold or even hostile towards another person before gradually showing a warm and caring side.
x: I usually draw very peaceful, happy manga, so it has been a real challenge for me to illustrate the vice president's death glare and Ri-chan's subtle tsundere attitude.
Even Kaname's rude and overbearing tsundere personality is explained by her having gone to school in the United States where she was socialized to just bluntly say what she thought.

s.d: Showing qualities typical of a tsundere.
x: Ah, the cactus. / Truly the most tsundere of plants.

tsuris.e: Borrowed from Yiddish צרות (tsores), plural of צרה (tsore, “trouble, problem”), from Hebrew צָרָה (tsará, “trouble, tragedy, calamity”).

s.d: (Yiddish) aggravating trouble
x: the frustrating tsuris he subjected himself to

s.d: (US, colloquial, uncountable) Problems or troubles.
x: You think you got troubles? You should go down there and talk to some of those schnorrers. Still, what chutzbah^([sic]). It's like the Jewish moral sense, emerging from all that tsuris.
“Sounds to me, my friend, like you got some tsuris. Not full grown yet, not gehoketh tsuris, but tsuris.”
